en: Preface to the *Zhongshu* (Exegesis on the Mediation) of the *Ullambana Sūtra*:

Those who cling to the literal words are constrained by their outward steps and may lose the profound meaning; those who exercise brilliant eloquence fall into empty abstractions and suffer from a failure to follow the sūtra.
As for that which is profoundly mysterious and brilliantly luminous, yet further accords with the teachings of the *Sūtras*, its principles are indeed precise.
In detail, he was perfectly suited to harmonize the finger with the moon beyond it, unifying the two subtleties to stand preeminent as a single school that walks alone.
Even the sages of old found this difficult; I have perused both the new and old commentaries on the *Ullambana Sūtra* and lament that the former worthies were unable to achieve mastery in both.
The old commentary relies on the sūtra for its exegesis, largely adhering to the phenomenal characteristics (*vastu-lakṣaṇa*) of the *Āgamas*.

The structural measurements are orderly and precise, yet the underlying meanings and implications beyond the words have not been fully revealed. The new commentary offers brilliant and versatile eloquence, and its literary style is rich and elegant;

its contemplation of principle is perfect and ultimate, yet it seems inconsistent with the manifest text. Furthermore, if "Single Dharma" is taken as the title, the two characters "Buddha-spoken" (佛說) are discarded;
if "Filial Piety and Compassion" is made the core tenet, the characters "Circulation" (流通) become redundant; and if "One Compassion" and the "Three Jewels" are taken as the essence...

I have striven to refine this discourse on the single vehicle while entirely forgetting my own limitations; having repeatedly read these texts, I could not bear that the Buddha’s scriptures remained obstructed.

Thus, without hesitation, I have summarized and clarified the flow of the argument, annotating the old commentaries to illuminate their essential meanings and correcting the new ones to bring them back into accord with the sūtras.
In this way, I hope that the text shall not lose its meaning and the exegesis shall not contradict the scripture.
In attempting to synthesize and uphold the vast, sacred transformation, how could one possibly merge these two wonders to form a single school?

Truly, I hope to attend to both principle and phenomena, moving with ease along the Middle Way. Now, one who studies the martial arts of Handan but fails to master the national technique may crawl upon the road;
how can they avoid the laughter of bystanders? It would be better to restrict one’s steps to that which requires no sacrifice. The ninth month of Wumu.

*A Concise Commentary on the Buddha-Spoken Ullambana Sūtra*.
Compiled by the Tiantai Bhikṣu Lingyao. △ I.
General Title: The Scripture on the Ullambana Bowl Spoken by the Buddha.
The commentary by one school explains that this sutra is titled according to its person and dharma, takes liberation as its essence,

takes great filial piety and the salvation of parents as its primary tenet, takes the eradication of suffering and the production of goodness as its function, and belongs to the *Vaipulya* (Extensive) class with the character of "fresh butter" (*navanīta*) within the teachings.

△ Regarding the explanation of the names: first, the specific name "Buddha" refers to the person who is the Śākyamuni Teacher, whose four analytical powers (catur-pratisaṃvid) flow forth in proclamation.

"Ullambana" is the Dharma, which is the essential purport of the sutra he taught. "Ullambana" is translated as "hanging upside down," while "pan" is a Chinese term still translated as "vessel for salvation.
The Sanskrit sound is often inverted; when read in its natural order, it is called "the vessel for saving those hanging upside down."

Now, first, let us explain the two characters "inverted suspension" (*dàoxuán*) by examining both their general and specific meanings according to principle and fact. Jia Yi’s "Treatise on Stabilizing the State" states:
"The situation of the empire is currently in an inverted suspension. This means that although a crown may be worn out, it is not used to cover a straw sandal;
and although a sandal may be new, it is not placed upon a crown. If the head were looking downward while the feet were looking upward, this would constitute an inverted suspension.

This sutra designates this state as "hanging upside down" because the six classes of ordinary beings, being deluded and failing to realize the truth, undergo the most extreme retribution for their heavy sins.
This is like being driven into the hells of the mountain of knives and trees of swords, or being sawn apart and weighed on scales;

for the most part, they receive their karmic retribution with their bodies and heads inverted. This is clarified among the mutual retributions of the six sense organs in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, where it describes the sinners.
The spirit and consciousness ride upon the void and enter hell like a fish leaping into a net; its head remains outside the net while its body is trapped within, entering by hanging upside down.

This hell is characterized by such inverted suspension. The *Tongji* records that one day during the night, Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty suffered the retribution of having a thousand fish heads upon his own, likewise with their heads hanging upside down inside a net—an instance of suffering within the realms of ghosts.
Those of heavy karma are also occasionally suspended by their necks as a form of retribution, much like humans caught in a snare.
In the past, someone visited the underworld and saw a ghost whose head had been removed and placed upside down by the roadside; these were all instances of ghosts being suspended upside down.
As for animals, they are called "those that walk sideways" (*tiryag-yoni*); thus, when their lives end, they are mostly slaughtered and hung upside down.
To weigh them by the head and sell them—as is generally understood for pigs, dogs, oxen, sheep, chickens, ducks, and pheasants—is the same even within the human realm;

though one may establish oneself through the bonds of human relations, if one commits crimes such as robbery, theft, lewdness, or murder, one will likewise be seized and subjected to the "inverted suspension" (daoxian) torture.
Thus, one knows that being suspended upside-down is reserved for those whose crimes are particularly grave.
It is not that this applies exclusively to the single class of hungry ghosts; this is a rough explanation based on the coarse level of karmic retribution regarding the six realms of ordinary beings.
One must know that when considered from the perspective of ultimate principle, it is profoundly clear that this extends all the way to the stage of Equal Enlightenment.

For retribution arises from karma, and karma arises from delusion; sentient beings mostly dwell in perversion and rarely dwell in non-perversion, yet within that state of non-perversion, they falsely give rise to [delusions].
With a perverted mind, there arise mental perversions, conceptual perversions, and view-perversions;

because of these delusive perversions, every action performed is nothing but perverse. For instance, among human beings, those who ought to be upright, righteous, filial toward their parents, and loyal to their sovereign instead commit the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes, being neither loyal nor filial, and even beating and reviling their parents.
To insult the worthy and the sages—is this not like a person who has inverted their body and head?
Even the bird *he-ju* (the pheasant-like *hede*), which desires to turn night into day, is loathed by humans and called "inverted";

how much more so for one whose conduct is perverse and contrary to nature, who ought naturally to receive the retribution of being suspended upside down? If one traces this back to its origin, it is all...
The true cause of sentient beings—the nature of numinous awareness—is from the beginning devoid of such designations as "correct" or "inverted," "distant" or "near.

Since even names cannot be maintained, how could there be any substantial reality? It is solely because of a single moment of non-awakening that movement arises; this is the ignorance of the "mark of birth.

From this, the three subtle states of karma, transformation, and manifestation arise. Thereupon, the six coarse states of grasping, attachment, and conceptual naming occur, like rivers flowing into the sea.
Their destinies descend lower and lower until they reach the Tailgate (Weilu), where they finally cease;

this constitutes the inverted, evil retribution of the six realms of ordinary beings—the karmic signs of bondage and the painful manifestations of suffering. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* meticulously investigates the seven destinies, stating:

"Within wondrous perfection, a single thought of delusion immediately forms the twelvefold wheel of inverted saṃsāra; from inversion comes birth. Regarding these inversions, there are those involving existence and...

If there is the cessation of perversion such that one can turn back from delusion and return to the correct, then within the wondrous perfection there is fundamentally no cyclic flow; therefore it is said:

"When the Tathāgata presses his finger, the Sea-Seal emits light, and he is named the Truly All-Knowing One. When you briefly raise your mind, the dust and toil arise first; this is called the perversion of nature.
The above concludes the explanation of the character for "perversion" (*diào*). "Hanging" (*xuán*) means "far away. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says:

It is a perilous and evil path of five hundred *yojanas*. Furthermore, it is said that the Buddha-way is still far off, and that those of you who belong to the Two Vehicles and are indolent cannot reach it.
It is also said that this person certainly knows the water is still far away;
having once returned to the right path, they travel further and further away, entering samsara in vain and unable to draw near. This is because even a single thought of this person—

The state of awakening is precisely where one is inverted and far removed; it does not necessarily require that the karmic suffering of the six realms of existence manifest before one can be said to be in a state of "hanging upside down.
Moreover, if one is merely suspended but not inverted, it may still be remedied; if one is inverted but not suspended, it may still be approached.
Now, however, one is both suspended and inverted, making it difficult to turn back the tide—like a criminal hung from a high beam.
One’s karma has already distanced one far from the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). If one were not inverted, one might perhaps stand upright;

but what can be done when both body and head are already overturned? If one were merely inverted but not suspended, one might perhaps rotate the hands and feet to turn the inversion back into the upright;
but what can be done when one is suspended high above a beam? When both sufferings entwine one thus, there is nothing that can be done.
This is like a person lost in their direction who wishes to reach Hunan but mistakenly heads toward the northern frontier.
If they do not move their feet at all, they are still not very far away; yet if they take even one step, they advance one step further from their goal.

Since every lifting of a foot and every movement of a step by an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is nothing other than transgression, how could they possibly proceed step by step from within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)? This is merely—
A brief explanation of the six ordinary beings' inverted suspension is now further analyzed through four propositions encompassing the nine realms:

First, the "inverted and suspended" proposition refers to the karma and suffering of ordinary beings. Second, the "near yet inverted" proposition refers to the adherence to truth and preservation of fruits by the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

This is because, having already perceived the ultimate truth (*satyadharma*), they claim to have entered the same *dharmatā*; thus, they travel from village to village and from kingdom to kingdom [seeking only their own liberation].
Upon arriving at the kingdom, he reached the city where his father resided; having already traveled three hundred *yojanas*, the place where the jewels were located was near.
Yet, being lost on the path to *nirvāṇa*, they speak of it as being far away.

Because they lack the aspiration to attain [the goal] and do not delight in it, those of the Two Vehicles are called "withered" regarding the four inversions. This was the case for Ānanda during the assembly at the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
To take the correct as inverted and the inverted as correct—this is what the Tathāgata calls "pitiable.
Third, the phrase "correct yet distant" refers to those of the Perfect Teaching (yuan-jen) who, at their initial stage, already know the secret treasury of the Tathāgata;

because they not only manifest the nine [stages] of the Buddha but also equally reveal them, they may be considered "correct. Yet, as they have not yet set out on the path and still remain [in that state],...

Because of these names, it is further called the "Distant Sutra. It says: "For example, when one digs a well and still sees dry earth, that person knows with certainty that the water is still far off.

Fourth is the phrase "both correct and near," which refers to the forty-one stages of the Grounds where the *tathāgatagarbha* has already been opened and the three virtues (*triguṇa*) are fully manifested.
The Sutra says: "By not ceasing one's efforts, one gradually reaches the mud. This is it.
If people know that water must be near when they see its vapor, how much more so for one who has fully opened their vision and fully realized the three virtues?
The four phrases [of the verse] exclude nothing. Once the fruit of wondrous enlightenment is attained, it no longer falls within the categories of correctness or inversion, nor proximity or distance;

for the nature of the spiritual awakening of the true cause of both sentient beings and Buddhas is fundamentally free from such designations as "correct" or "inverted. Thus, the Sūtra says: "It is far removed."
This refers to inverted dreams and delusions. Furthermore, it should be understood that the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) are categorized under the "inverted and near" phrase;

this is stated from the perspective of mutual comparison. If one contrasts the Perfect [Teaching] alone with the preceding three, then all three of the former are considered "inverted and suspended," as the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa says in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "From before this point, we were all called those of false views."

Regarding humans, the *Gaoseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks) states that a person of perfect enlightenment (*yuanren*) is pervasive throughout their entire being and free from deviance, crookedness, partiality, or inversion;

even a Bodhisattva is still said to possess the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*), as they have not yet opened the central reality (*zhongshi*). Prior to this, all were in a state of inverted delusion.
Nevertheless, although the forty-one stages of the person of perfect enlightenment may be considered nearly correct, they are not yet so, for ignorance (*avidyā*) has not [yet been exhausted].
All of these are the inversion of delusion; the outflowing and non-outflowing karmas are the inversion of karma; and the birth-and-death of transformation is the inversion of suffering.

Within the land of true retribution, the five sense objects are sublime and wonderful, yet they are the same as the "love of the same substance. It is only in the ninth stage that one cultivates the pure dhyāna free from views;
even at the stage of Equal Enlightenment, there remains a single grade of the ignorance of the mark of arising, which is precisely the first moment of non-enlightenment.

Yet there exists the delusive appearance of movement; this delusion is precisely an inversion that distances one from the true cause—the numinous awareness—and though one may still possess the tether of a single lifetime, it is like being bound by a rope.
Though not yet hanging upside down from a high beam, fully fettered by the five corpses, how could one who has a rope tied around the neck not be a guilty person?
Therefore, explaining "hanging upside down" in terms of concrete phenomena refers only to the six [realms].

In general, explaining this principle through the metaphor of being "suspended upside down" extends all the way to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*Samyaksambodhi*) before the meaning of the sutra is fully exhausted.
Next, regarding the term "rescuer," it is another name for one who provides liberation. Jia Yi, the Grand Tutor, said: "If one is suspended upside down like this, no one can rescue them.
Mencius said: "In the present age, when a ruler of ten thousand chariots practices benevolent government, the people's joy in it is like being rescued from being suspended upside down."

The essential point of this "Hanging" [Sūtra] is that its primary purpose is to universally rescue all beings from the suffering of being inverted and suspended, encompassing both principle and phenomena, as well as general and specific cases.
As the Sūtra says: "All self-restrained sages and worthies have realized the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); their virtue is vast and expansive.
Consequently, after receiving the food, Maudgalyāyana’s mother immediately attained liberation from all the sufferings of the hungry ghosts, and so forth.

The celestial flower-light canopy arises because ordinary beings, through inverted views, construct conditioned mental activities and thereby create conditioned evil karma, which brings about the retribution of inverted suspension as suffering.
Now, by means of the unconditioned sagely virtue, one can immediately dissolve the suffering of conditioned karma;
how much more so in the case of Maudgalyāyana’s mother, whose previous roots of stinginess and greed brought forth this retribution, but who now possesses joy and renunciation.
The untainted [state] is precisely that which can oppose and destroy its obstacles; this treatise rescues the six classes of ordinary beings from their inverted suspension. The Sūtra says:
"I shall now expound the Dharma of rescue so that all who are in difficulty may be freed from sorrow and suffering.

Are those in difficulty not precisely those who have reached up to Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) and are bound by the single lifetime? Is it not the case that they are all freed from sorrow and suffering?
Is this not the suffering of the transformative birth-and-death (*pariṇāma-vaiparītya*) produced by external conditions within the realm beyond sudden extinction?

Indeed, the mere four characters "detached from all" (*sarva-vivikta*) are sufficient to show that the Tathāgata did not preach this single sutra solely for the sake of removing the inverted suspension of the six realms of ordinary beings.
As the saying goes: "A crossbow capable of launching a thousand-jin bolt does not release its trigger for a field mouse. This is the Dharma King of myriad virtues.
One should not interpret even the superficial aspects of the Buddhadharma for ordinary people using only shallow meanings;
how much less so when there are explicit words of ultimate profundity that could instead be reduced to the mere phenomena of the Āgamas?
If one claims that this sutra contains few passages of deep discourse and thus interprets it only superficially, does not a single word from the Son of Heaven constitute a decree?

Yaśas asked: "How can those who are liberated through the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—whose merit does not exceed that of self-indulgent bhikṣus—save those dwelling on the earth from their inverted understanding?
He replied: "One must know that although the unconditioned dharma is one, there are distinctions of depth and shallowness.

Here, the unconditioned liberation of the two vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha) saves those who are inverted by the provisional characteristics of the six sense objects; however, it is the merit of the unconditioned of the Perfect Vehicle (Ekayāna) [that truly liberates]."
To rescue those dwelling on the earth from the perversity of inverted views, it is as if a Great Being has temporarily manifested among the bhikṣus.
It is clearly stated that while he is inwardly secret, he manifests outwardly; his original lofty traces are hidden beneath humble conduct—how could they be fathomed?

Or perhaps he is one who, having already realized wondrous enlightenment, has personally shattered the conditioned inversions of the mark of birth, and whose perfect primary cause and numinous awakening are titled "Right Universal Knowledge" (Samyak-saṃbuddha); such a one has now come.

On this assembly, one is immediately able to universally shatter the signs of birth within the nine realms and the conditioned existence, and universally rescue those bound by the suffering of the stage of Equal Enlightenment and other such delusions;
therefore it is said that the Way of the Multitude of Sages possesses a virtue as vast as the ocean.

Being thus vast, one has already reached the ultimate ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), and is able to universally deliver the deluded and inverted beings of the nine realms in every thought-moment. If one does not act in this way—
To explain this: if one says "all are removed," it becomes a redundant expression; for a Great Being’s skillful manifestation has no fixed purpose.
○ A basin (*pén*) is simply a vessel, and a vessel is simply a basin; the meanings in Chinese and Sanskrit are identical, so there is no need for confusion or alteration.

Whether one uses a bowl (*wǎn*) as in the Eastern Land, or an alms-bowl (*pātra*) as in the Western Regions, or a basin or a cup—whichever it may be, provided it can hold food to offer to the Triple Gem, that is sufficient.
This ear is like a cloud; when all share the same mind in receiving the *pātra-bhara* (alms) meal, it naturally does not require the formal arrangement of seats (*zhuìpán*) for the assembly.
The above is a specific title of the sutra, while [the following] is its general designation.

If one applies the specific case to the general, there should be different categories of sutras concerning teaching, practice, and principle, as detailed in the *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra*. Whether translated or untranslated, [the classification remains].

The fifteen meanings are fully detailed in the *Myōhuan* (Excellence of the Profound). I now maintain that this sutra’s teachings on the Dharma and its teachings on permanence are sufficient to exhaustively encompass its meaning.

Since the Tathāgata’s body serves as the teacher for the nine realms and his words serve as the law for all under heaven, and since he preached this excellent method for rescuing his mother from her inverted suspension to the Honored One of that time, it must likewise serve as a bridge and raft for future generations; thus, it shall endure for a thousand autumns.
The following is the constant rule for filial sons and virtuous grandsons in repaying their kin and honoring their origins. The Sūtra states:

"On the fifteenth day of the seventh month each year, the day of the monks' *pravāraṇā*, one should cultivate the *bālambana* offering. This has been transmitted from generation to generation without interruption until the present;
is this not indeed the sublime and eternal path? Therefore, it is named the "Sūtra," while the new commentary relies solely on the Dharma.
If one were to take "offering" as the title, then the two characters "Buddha-spoken" (佛說) would be discarded as if they belonged to a person exiled to the wilderness;
how could this be the constant and unchanging interpretation of the seven types of titles?

If one examines the provenance of this sutra, it was translated during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Western Jin by Dharmarakṣa (竺法護); since his name was *Dharmarakṣa* (曇摩羅剎), people thus called it [after him].
The Dharma Master Fashu was originally from the Yuezhi people; he came to the Eastern Land and resided in Dunhuang before moving to Chang’an’s Qingmen Gate.
The translator was none other than the person who produced the present-day *Ullambana Sūtra* (Yulanpen jing) spoken by the Buddha.
As for the *Guanla jing* (or alternatively called the *Ba’en jing*) translated by Faju, it was a later re-translation and is not the current version. This concludes the explanation of the names.
If one discusses the essence of the sutra, it consists of three kinds of liberation. The sutra states:
"If one can make offerings to this Sangha of those who observe the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, their parents and six types of kinsmen shall attain liberation at that very moment.

If they were merely liberated from the inverted suffering of the six classes of ordinary beings, this would be the solitary liberation of the two vehicles, lacking the perfection of both body and wisdom. [However,] if all hardships are removed and sorrow and suffering are directly...

"Saving the world while dwelling in the inverted position" refers to the perfection of the three gates of liberation; this is the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the *Hundred Verses on Liberation*, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Furthermore, this root scripture is also called the *Devapuṣpaprakāśa* (Light of Heavenly Flowers), which is an alternative name for the perfection of the three gates of liberation.
The ultimate heaven (*paramārtha-dhātu*) inherently possesses the *prajñā* of the Great Radiant Treasury (*mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*), which serves as its light; moreover, it further possesses—

The flowers of the causes of the myriad practices collectively adorn the fruit of virtue; thus, the Flower-Light (Huaguang) is inseparable from the Dharma-Heaven (Yitian), and the Dharma-Heaven necessarily possesses the Flower-Light.
To mention one, all three are present; though there are three, they are one. If these three are separated, they become nine; yet when combined, their fundamental source is one.

If one applies this principle of perfect liberation to the categories of defilement and purity, it then corresponds directly to the three paths, the three consciousnesses, the three natures, and the three types of beings.

If the three types of enlightenment (*sambodhi*), the three Great Vehicles, the three types of nirvāṇa, and the Three Jewels (*triratna*) with their three virtues are not all of one essence and nothing but different names,
then taking this perfect liberation as the essence accords with the extant text and encompasses all interpretations.
As for the *Xinshu* (New Commentary) discarding "liberation" and forcibly taking the Three Jewels as the essence— this is something I have never heard before.
Now, this sutra aims precisely to rescue hungry ghosts from the suffering of inverted suspension caused by their karmic bonds;
it takes liberation as its essence. First, it serves as an antidote to those karmic bonds; second, it facilitates the removal of fetters and the return to liberation. Therefore, the sutra states:

"Those who make offerings to the Sangha during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony shall have their parents and six types of relatives liberated at that very moment. This explicit text is clear and undeniable. Why is this so?
If one does not rely upon [this] or abandons this essence, one will be like a blind person without a guide, wandering aimlessly—where would one go?

Furthermore, from what scriptural passage does the establishment of the Three Jewels as the essence derive? If it refers to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, there is the expression "the Dharma-nature *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*";
if it refers to the *Samantabhadra-darśana*, there is the instruction to "read and recite the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras."

In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, there are passages concerning the use of mantras to rescue those from calamity; however, this present scripture merely speaks of making offerings to monks during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.

It does not mention the Buddha extending his supernatural power to go and rescue hungry ghosts, nor does it describe which sūtra should be recited, which mantra upheld, or what esoteric or exoteric spiritual chapter should be relied upon to rescue those bound by karma who hang head-downward like an inverted vase. Such methods for rescuing these beings currently exist [in other texts].

To discard the very essence of liberation and instead forcibly adopt an incomplete set of the Three Jewels to block one's own purity—this must be because the Master [Daoxuan] himself composed the *Ullambana Sūtra*, thereby making what exists non-existent and what does not exist existent.
If it were claimed that this sūtra possesses the meaning of the Three Jewels, then every sūtra would likewise possess the Three Jewels; thus, [the sūtra]...

Must all sutras take the Three Jewels as their essence? For example, the Lotus Sutra never fails to embody the Three Jewels, yet it takes the ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*) it expounds as its essence;
the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra likewise never fails to embody the Three Jewels, yet it takes the Prajñā it expounds as its essence.
Even if this sutra were to embody the Three Jewels, it should properly take the liberation (*vimukti*) it expounds as its essence.

How can one discard the manifest explanation of liberation and instead establish a generic, universal Three Jewels? Examining this, it is known that this commentary’s establishment of the essence (tǐ) commits two errors:

When the Zhou dynasty moved east, the Master [Confucius] appeared; when the Song dynasty moved south, [the Sage] emerged.

Yet, when Duke Wen rose from a time of extreme evil and exile, had not great sages and worthies been born among them to serve as capping pillars against the wild waves and silently pull back the collapsing winds, both the Way of the world and the Buddha-dharma would have utterly perished.
Furthermore, the sutra states, "It is not within the power of you alone to do anything about it," which serves to distinguish and clarify two subsequent meanings.
"If you cannot manage this within yourself, how can you know that even sages and worthies find it difficult?

How much more so for the multitude of ordinary beings, including those of heaven, earth, spirits, and ghosts? This selection [of whom to save] is not something you can accomplish with your own power alone;
it is evident that only through the power of the myriad sages of the ten directions can they be rescued and delivered. △ Second, the difficulty of rescuing the multitude of ordinary beings.
Although your filial piety has moved heaven and earth, neither the spirits and deities of heaven and earth, nor the malevolent spirits, heretics, Daoist masters,
or the gods of the Four Heavenly Kings can do anything to you.
Yet, since even Maudgalyāyana— the Arhat of the Samādhis— cannot fathom the realm of humans and devas, Maudgalyāyana cannot save you now.
How could this be something within the reach of ordinary, common people? △ Second, the actual demonstration of the method for saving others, in three parts:

first, the simultaneous presentation of both [the person and the method], second, the simultaneous demonstration of both, and third, the simultaneous conclusion of both. The first part has two sub-sections; the first is the presentation of the person.
"One must rely on the majestic spiritual power of the Sangha of the ten directions to attain liberation.
The two characters "dāng xū" (當須) are not redundant; rather, they signify "to hope for" or "to require.

This means that one must necessarily rely on the majestic spiritual power of the various sages, hoping thereby to receive healing and salvation; without this, it would be impossible to cause them to attain liberation. [The phrase continues: "The ten directions..."

If one interprets the term "Saṃgha" (the Sangha) as the opposite of what was explained above, then the "Ten Directions" reveals that it is not merely a single holy being, and the "Sangha" reveals that they are not ordinary worldlings;
thus, their majestic power can reach everywhere, even to those who are suspended upside down, so that they may be liberated.

Since the person capable of saving has already been identified, yet it is not known by what Dharma one might move these holy beings to obtain such salvation, the text immediately presents the Dharma capable of saving below.
It says: "△ Second, the indication of the Dharma.
'I shall now proclaim the Dharma of deliverance so that all beings in distress may be freed from sorrow and suffering.
Previously it said 'one must,' and now it says 'I shall proclaim'; these two instances of the character *dāng* (shall/must) clarify that this indicates both the person and the Dharma."
This is the correct explanation of the Dharma capable of saving beings. "All difficulties" refers to the sin of being suspended upside down;
this state of being suspended upside down occurs not only among the class of hungry ghosts (*preta*), but extends even to those bound by a single lifetime.

Thus it is said that "all" [suffering] is like the alternating pain and pleasure of humans and devas, where one cannot escape the calamities of war and, failing to attain the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*), will inevitably fall into the difficulty of being suspended upside down.
Furthermore, the two vehicles drink the wine of ignorance and fall into the pit of quiescent extinction; this is the peril of being perversely suspended.

Bodhisattvas are preoccupied with the two truths and lose the foundation of the Middle Way, falling into the peril of being perversely suspended between the two extremes. Those at the stages of the *bhūmis*, the *vihāras*, and Equal Enlightenment have not yet eliminated the mark of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*);
because the cause shifts and the fruit changes, they face the peril of being perversely suspended. Within each of these nine realms of peril, every one of them possesses [these dangers].

Regarding the two matters of *daurmanasya* (sorrow) and *duḥkha* (suffering), as the *Xinshu* (New Commentary) states: "Mental sensation is termed *daurmanasya*, while bodily sensation is termed *duḥkha*.

To fear future retribution is called *daurmanasya*; to be beset by present conditions is called *duḥkha*. To lack the means for deliverance is called *daurmanasya*; to have pain cutting one's very skin is called *duḥkha*.
Thus, we know that the "calamity of being suspended upside down" is the general name, while *daurmanasya* and *duḥkha* are the two distinct aspects.
When the Tathāgata’s Dharma-gate is proclaimed once, it not only saves the Venerable One’s mother but also saves all sentient beings within the nine realms;

it not only uproots the calamities of the hungry ghosts but also uproots the anxieties and sufferings of the two deaths. Therefore, it is said: "It causes all those in distress to be free from sorrow and suffering.
△ Second, the dual demonstration, which has two parts: first, the actual presentation of the person and the Dharma; second, the extensive explanation.
Praising the Virtues and Benefiting the Beginning; furthermore, this section has two parts. First, identifying the person:

the Buddha told Maudgalyāyana that on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when the monastic community of the ten directions performs the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination), this specifically identifies the person capable of saving others.
Furthermore, it must coincide with the necessary temporal conditions; only when these factors are fully harmonized can such a superior matter be accomplished.

Regarding the time for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism): every fourteenth day of the fourth month, the Buddha ordained that bhikṣus enter the summer retreat (*varṣā*) to diligently cultivate their spiritual practice.
When the ninety-day period—comprising the three days of the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth of the seventh month—is completed, they conclude the retreat and perform the *pravāraṇā*.
If there is an intercalary month, one hundred and twenty days constitute a single summer retreat; if there is an intercalary fourth month, the preceding fourth month [is used].
On the sixteenth day, the summer retreat (varṣā) is entered; even if there is an intercalary seventh month, the retreat is concluded in the preceding seventh month.
Within this single summer, one may attain the four dhyānas, the four fruits [of the śrāvaka], samādhis, and supernormal powers (abhijñā)—these are beyond counting.

Should there be those who have not yet attained the realization of the fruits, it is not that they lack flaws in their three karmas. Since those involved themselves remain deluded, they must rely on an outside observer to point out their errors.
Therefore, one must allow the assembly of monks to freely point out and speak of all the transgressions one has committed; only then can one repent and become pure.

This *pravāraṇā* (Sanskrit for *bāla-varaṇa*) is the term for the invitation to speak freely. The formula for the invitation is as follows: "Venerable assembly of monks, today is the day of *pravāraṇā*.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], also invite you to speak freely. If the Venerable Ones see, hear, or suspect any offense in me,"
"Venerable sirs, out of compassion for me, please speak; if I see my faults, I shall confess them according to the Dharma.
Having said this three times in succession, once the *pravāraṇā* has been received, it is called the completion of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat).
Since this is the occasion when the Great Saṅgha assembles in harmony to exert themselves in the Noble Path—a most auspicious gathering—one should seek [this assembly] to rescue one's parents.
△ Second, showing the Dharma:
One should prepare for one's parents of seven lifetimes past and those currently undergoing calamities and hardships, a meal of a hundred flavors, the five fruits,
vessels for water and rinsing, fragrant oil, lamps and candles, beds and bedding, and all the sweet delicacies of the world, placing them within the basin.
The midday offering is made to the assembly of virtuous monks of the ten directions.
By universally making offerings to the sages and worthies in this way, one can extricate the suffering of the inverted suspension within the Dharma-realm.

Although among those being saved there may be parents, it is the sages and worthies who are truly capable of saving them; yet, because the primary intention lies in the offering of the Dharma, it is called "showing the Dharma."

"Providing food of a hundred flavors and the like" is the specific opening regarding the offering substances; "exhausting all the world's sweets and delicacies" is the general summary of the method of offering.
The five fruits are: first, stone fruits such as peaches and plums; second, skin-fruits such as melons and pears; third, shell-fruits such as walnuts and pomegranates;
fourth, pulp-fruits such as sesame and castor-oil seeds; and fifth, horn-fruits such as water chestnuts and beans. These exhaust all the world's sweets.
The character "exhaustion" (jin) is interpreted in two senses, which is quite comprehensive: when wealthy, one gathers the rare treasures of the world;
when poor, one exhausts the full measure of one's own strength. One must know that making offerings to the Sages and seeking their salvation fundamentally value the utmost sincerity;
the Three Honored Ones accept offerings only in response to such sincerity, regardless of the abundance of the material objects.

Regarding frugality, the Book of Documents says: "The spirits do not always accept offerings; they accept those characterized by sincerity. When supreme governance is fragrant, it moves the divine intelligences;

it is not the millet and grain that are fragrant, but the brilliant virtue that is fragrant. If this is true even for ghosts and spirits, how much more so for the Triple Gem? Furthermore, it says: "Offerings consist largely of ritual propriety;

if the offering does not reach the substance, it is because the offering is incomplete. Thus, even if one were to be cautious regarding extravagance and expand [the ritual], [it would still be insufficient].
If even the deities would spit out offerings of carved metal and embroidered silks, how much more so the sages and worthies?
The responsibility for offerings made through the application of mind lies with the monastic community; the duty for offerings made with sincere devotion belongs to the lay populace.

Only when one can thus rescue the Dharma-offering by ensuring both the practice and the principle are refined can it be considered truly appropriate. As for those items placed within the basin, they pertain to both the Eastern and Western Lands.

Vessels and utensils differ; whether they be objects, bowls, or made of gold, silver, porcelain, or wood, provided they can hold things to offer to the sages and worthies, there is no restriction on their number—one may use even a thousand or ten thousand of them.
This is precisely what is called the *bowl-umbrella-offering* (*alabana-pūjā*).
The subsequent phrase, "with one mind receiving the *pātra-hāra* meal," also specifically refers to this. The term for "virtuous elder" (*dàdé*) is the Sanskrit word *dāna*.

"Tatha" is a venerable title for bhikṣus within the Vinaya. The previous statement said "the Sangha of the ten directions," whereas the present says "to make offerings to the assembly of Great Virtuous (Mahā-śrāvaka) monks of the ten directions.
To speak of them as "Great Virtuous" reveals that they are not mere beginners or those of shallow learning;

to speak of them as "Great Virtuous" implies they must possess the power of majestic spiritual authority; to speak of them as "Great Virtuous" indicates they are capable of rescuing those suffering from the agony of being hung upside down.
It is said that only those of Great Virtue (*bhadanta*) are able to bestow the bliss of liberation. Even a single character from the *Ratnarāja-sūtra* written in ink cannot fully express this;

how much less so when it encompasses all these various meanings? △ Second, the extensive praise of the virtues and benefits. Above, the method by which he can rescue sentient beings has been explained in detail;
however, one may wonder what kind of majestic power these sages and worthies possess that excels even the Buddha’s own eyes.
Even those who offer their last rites can be rescued from the suffering of being suspended upside down and attain the joy of liberation;

yet those who receive this benefit do not know whether it was in one lifetime or many lifetimes. Therefore, he follows this by extolling the virtues [of the Buddha] and demonstrating the benefits obtained, in order to inspire the hearts of both monastics and laypeople with faith, joy, and enthusiasm, so that they may move him with sincerity and devotion.

To manifest that all the sages have long possessed the fundamental capacity for bestowing salvation and that their resonance has thus become unimpeded, there are two parts: first, a praise of their virtues.
On this day, some among the multitude of sages were in mountain retreats in meditative concentration; some had attained the fruits of the four paths; some were walking in meditation beneath trees;
some exercised mastery over the six supernormal powers to teach and transform śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; and some were bodhisattvas of the ten stages.
The Great Being, manifesting as a bhikṣu through his skillful means, was in the midst of the great assembly;
all were of one mind receiving the *pātra-piṇḍapāta* (alms-food), possessing the path of the holy community with pure precepts, their virtue vast and profound.

The phrase "all the assembly of noble ones" is the general heading, indicating that they are all of one mind. What follows below is the concluding praise; the middle section is the detailed explanation.
From "mountain retreats and meditative concentration" up to "sovereign teaching and transformation" is the exposition of the methods for cultivation and realization.

From "śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas" downwards clarifies the persons capable of realization. "Dhyāna" refers to the joy and bliss born of seclusion, the joy and bliss born of concentration, and the joy and bliss born of seclusion.

The four dhyānas—consisting of joy, bliss, equanimity, and pure mindfulness—and the four formless attainments—namely, the infinity of space, the infinity of consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception—constitute the fundamental meditative concentrations of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
The four fruits of the path are realized by the Śrāvakas of the Small Vehicle outside the triple world; thus, their practice of walking meditation beneath trees pertains to the state of an Ārya.
Whether great or small, those who possess mastery over the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) in their teaching and transformation must point toward the forty-two stages of the Mahāyāna.
These six supernormal powers are: the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, mastery over the body, and the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Sentient beings, from within a single essence of spiritual clarity, divide it into six combined functions; consequently, the ear does not transcend sound, and the eye does not exceed form.
Each and every obstruction is not independent; for the worthies and sages of the Three Vehicles, once there is understanding, the six [senses] are lost.

The six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are supreme, each and every one interpenetrating and being none other than liberation. Therefore it is said that the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are sovereign.

Thus one knows that these six are interpenetrating, their nature being inherently complete; even when the fruit is realized, they return to their source. Why? Because within the darkness, one must exert oneself diligently.
Reading with clarity and without delusion such that the moment a thought arises there is nothing seen—this is the nature of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

Hearing the movement of ants beneath one’s bed as if they were clashing chariots—this is the nature of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*). Knowing the thoughts of one’s mother or others—this is the nature of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*).

Recalling past lives—this is the nature of recollecting former existences (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*). Shooting an arrow through stone so it sinks in, or casting iron into the forge so it becomes gold—this is the nature of the supernormal power of the feet (*ṛddhipāda*).
One does not drink from the spring of skulls, nor does one weary of seeing the ghosts who demand debts; this is the nature of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
All ordinary beings fundamentally possess the nature of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*); thus, once the fetters are severed, all six become sovereign.
This is because the nature of the six sovereign kings is pure. Therefore, after the fruition is realized, one is able to manifest transformations infinitely.
With inconceivable supernormal powers, they extensively perform Buddha-works to transform and guide all beings; as described in the *Avataṃsaka*,
they may enter meditative absorption through a single sense-faculty and emerge from it by speaking through all faculties,
or enter absorption through all faculties and emerge from it by speaking through a single faculty, or enter absorption through the ear-faculty and emerge from it through the eye-faculty.
Emerging from meditative absorption to speak, whether entering absorption through the eye-faculty and emerging through the tongue-faculty,
or entering absorption within a male body and emerging within a female body—
is this not the dharma-gate cultivated and practiced by the great beings of the ten stages and the noble ones of the forty-two positions? If one is ignorant of this...
If one were to explain this according to the [conventional] texts, the phrase "teaching with mastery over the six supernormal powers" would be difficult to reconcile.
The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas constitute the Two Vehicles; the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages constitute the Mahāyāna.

By mentioning only the Ten Stages, both the Separate (Beban) and Perfect (En) schools—comprising the forty-two stages of the fundamental severance—are encompassed. The manifested Bhikṣu was among the great assembly.
Just as Maitreya and Avalokiteśvara currently sit among the ranks of bhikṣus, or perhaps within the ranks of those of Equal and Sublime Enlightenment,

they conceal their original lofty traces while manifesting humble appearances; because they accept offerings, they are able to perfectly uproot the suffering of the inverted suspension of the nine realms and the three vehicles,
universally bestowing the bliss of liberation through the three virtues of the Buddha-realm— how much more so for the inverted suspension of the realm of segmented birth!
Is it not simply that one leaves behind the suffering of the human realm and enters the bliss of the Heavenly Flower Radiance? Thus, he concludes by saying:

"All share the same mind in receiving the *pātra-bhara* (alms-food); one must know that while there is no differentiation in the unconditioned Dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), there are distinctions of noble and ordinary, great and small.
Nevertheless, the mind with which they receive the food is without difference; how much more so when they share the same non-..."

The Dharma for this purpose is the same: the fundamentally pure original enlightenment (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-āśraya*). Once this One is realized, all matters are completed. Outside of this One, there is no dharma;
when the true mark (*dharmatā*) of the mind manifests, suffering is not something to be extracted and happiness is not something to be bestowed.

Although the one mind has no dualistic characteristics, it does not hinder the operation of great compassion of the same substance (*samatā-kāya-mahākaruṇā*), which universally extracts the suffering of the *dharmadhātu* and bestows the happiness of the *dharmadhātu*. This is...
Because it uproots the foundation of being suspended upside down, one should fully demonstrate the path of the multitude of sages endowed with pure precepts;

its virtue is vast and expansive. These three phrases are the general verses of praise. It is not improper to analyze them according to the categories of precept, concentration, and wisdom. The Great Sūtra states:
"There is the awakened pure precept that fulfills the unsurpassed path. This precept is the light of the primary truth (*paramārtha*).
This light is neither blue, yellow, red, nor white; it is neither form, nor mind, nor the dharma of cause and effect—it is the ultimate reality-mark of the precepts.
It is the path of the various sages. "Sage" (sheng) means "correct" (zheng). The minds of ordinary beings wander among the realms of sensory dust, and all such states are termed "deviant.
If one enters samādhi, it is called the sphere of correct mental activity, and is also termed the "Assembly of Correct Concentration" (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi). As for the word "path" (dao):
A "road" (lu) is that by which one proceeds; what is called a "path" (dao) is that by which one goes toward a destination.

Thus, among the sages of the Three Vehicles, none do not rely on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to give rise to wisdom (*prajñā*). To designate concentration as the "right path" and wisdom as the "ultimate virtue," the terminology is perfectly clear.
That virtue is vast and expansive—virtue means "attainment. It refers to being sufficient within oneself, having no dependence on the external.

This is what is called "virtue" (*guṇa*). When the wisdom of the four teachings and the four noble truths is cultivated, one is able to realize and exhaustively penetrate both principles of Truth and the Middle Way, reaching the ultimate shore of *nirvāṇa*.
This is already arriving home, where there is no further dependence on cultivating other dharmas.

"Vast and expansive" (*yanghuang*) refers to the state of water being so immense and boundless; when the virtues of the four truths of arising and ceasing are perfected, it is called "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*).

There are those who attain the Way through the four *śrotāpatti* (streams) of both "is" and "neither is nor is not"; these belong to the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) and they claim to have entered the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) together with the Buddha.
This is like the autumn water; though it is profound, before one has truly attained it, it is merely called vast and expansive.

The Four Truths of Non-arising are like a river, while the Four Truths of the Immeasurable are like a great river; compared to the former, the latter appears vast and boundless, yet even this, when compared to what follows, is still but a small stream.

If one’s views remain narrow, they cannot be called vast. Only when the forty-two great beings who manifest through expedient means cultivate the wisdom of the four noble truths of non-action, thereby perfectly shattering ignorance and fully revealing the secret treasury, flowing spontaneously into the ocean of *sarvajñā* and reaching the ultimate shore of *nirvāṇa*, can their virtue finally be described as "vast. This is merely a provisional explanation.
To explain his own practice: if we discuss his transformation of others and his uprooting [of suffering], it is called "virtue" (*guṇa*) because he gives rise to goodness.
The Sage himself has already realized the ultimate ocean of wisdom; furthermore, he turns the Dharma-gates practiced by his own mind to benefit others.

Thus, he is like a vast expanse of water capable of universally rescuing those in the nine realms who are withered and parched, suspended head-downward in the two deaths—far exceeding the rescue provided by a house on fire.
It is merely that they have slightly revived and found coolness upon the ground.
Furthermore, by means of this water, the Dharma-body of wondrous enlightenment and the fruits of all-knowledge across the forty-one stages for sentient beings of the nine realms will be restored;

it is not merely a matter of withered sprouts flourishing again or parched ruts flowing once more. Since the Bodhisattva has already perfected such a wondrous realization, he offers this to uproot suffering.
This is indeed appropriate. △ Second, showing the benefits: 3. Liberation of deceased parents.

Those who make offerings to this Sangha of self-indulgence (svairacārin) shall find that their parents and six types of kinsmen and relatives in the present life are liberated from the sufferings of the three evil paths;
they shall attain liberation at that very moment, and food and clothing will come to them spontaneously.
"Parents of the present life" refers to those whose fundamental karma for this current birth has already been exhausted and who have passed away.
This is verified by the subsequent phrase, "if parents are currently living," which indicates that these are those who have already returned to the realm of the dead (*mīng*).
Because they are offered to the Holy Ones, they escape the three miserable realms; "at the appropriate time" (*yìngshí*) means immediately. Thus, people [attain liberation].
If one makes offerings before their death, the deceased will immediately ascend to the underworld;

this is precisely the inconceivable power of the mutual resonance between the Way and its response, wherein Guanyin does not come and the practitioner does not go—just as water remains in the basin while the moon stays in the sky.

However, if one offers to the sages and worthies of the Two Vehicles, they may deliver the deceased from the three miserable realms, whether through liberation at a specific time or liberation independent of time.

The liberation of solitary tuning is the liberation through provisionality; if one serves a great person who manifests through skillful means, one will surely sever the two deaths, the three delusions, and the birth-phase ignorance, thereby attaining true-nature liberation.
This liberation is exclusively Perfect (Yuan) and must necessarily possess both body and wisdom. To mention one is to include all three;

to speak of the three is to include the one. Furthermore, the three dharmas—namely, the Way (Dao), consciousness (shi), and so forth—constituting the ten types, serve as the foundation for this sutra.
The "essence" (tǐ) referred to as the "correct essence" (zhèng tǐ) specifically points to liberation (*vimukti*), thereby more clearly manifesting the accomplishment of the fruit:

an awakened awareness that has emerged from the entanglements, rather than merely the true reality (*dharmatā*) within delusion or the primordial *dharmakāya*. If this essence were absent, erroneous inversion would lack its seal and would become the teaching of a demon (*māra*).

As it says below, [this essence] is the same substance as the "Heavenly Flower Radiance" (*Tianhuaguang*), differing only in name. The *Xinshu* (New Commentary) identifies the Three Jewels as the essence; this is not [the case here].
It is natural. Regarding "naturalness of clothing and food": meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is the clothing and wisdom (*prajñā*) is the food.
Adorned with these, one cultivates the path of effort through skillful means and conditions to perfect the *dharmakāya*.

When one abides naturally beyond this stage, superior wisdom and merit increase daily while the cessation of defilements (*prahāṇa*) diminishes daily; flowing spontaneously into the state of effortless spontaneity (*anabhoga*), it is only then called "self-nature."
Indeed. △ Second, increasing the happiness of present parents:
if one's parents are currently living, they shall enjoy blessings and happiness for a hundred years.
△ Third, the transformation-birth of parents throughout seven generations.
If one's parents of seven generations have been reborn in heaven through spontaneous birth (*upapāduka*), they enter the celestial Flower-Radiance.

While all devas are born spontaneously, those whose palaces are made of flowers were once flower-gatherers who, after dying, were reborn in heavenly palaces where their dwellings were entirely composed of flowers, as described in the *Fayuan zhulin* (Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma). All devas possess bodies.
Because the light brings him personal joy, it is said that he "enters the Heavenly Flower Light. This is an explanation based on conventional phenomena (*dharma*).
If we discuss the holy sages to whom offerings are made—who are all great beings manifesting through skillful means—then the benefit gained here is not merely that of the human or celestial realms;

rather, "Heaven" refers to Great Nirvana, the Supreme Heaven among heavens, the Heaven of the Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha*). "Flower" refers to liberation, the myriad practices, and the conditions for enlightenment (*pratyaya-hetu*); these are the general names.
The *Sūtra on the Great Assembly of the Fruits and Virtues Adorned with Flowers* states: "Samādhi is the stamen and liberation is the unfolding petals;

the petals are the flowers, and the light is Prajñā. This so-called light of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is not blue, yellow, red, or white, yet it is the great treasury of radiant light (*mahā-ābhāsaraśmi-garbha*) that can universally illuminate all.
One should know that this is precisely the perfectly wondrous treasury of the three liberations (*trivimokṣa*).

This scripture explains that it is called "Entry" (*praveśa*) because it elucidates through discourse and debate the immeasurable merits—the various practices of the true essence—which all converge and return to a single point, thereby adorning them. However, as for this "entry," there is nothing to enter into;
as the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "The wisdom that enters into principle is called 'abiding,' for one abides in prajñā by means of the dharma of non-abiding."

Among the *pāramitās*, one now enters the secret treasury of the three virtues by means of non-entry. Interpreting it in this way alone exhausts the majestic spiritual power of the sages and great beings;
only then can it be called "causing all things difficult to transcend to leave behind sorrow and suffering.

If a shallow scripture is given a profound interpretation, its merit is already beyond measure; yet if a profound Dharma is discussed with shallow understanding, I fear it violates the Buddha’s intent.

△ Third, having already extensively explained above the methods for saving sentient beings as well as the merits of the sages and worthies, what follows merely summarizes the remaining points not yet exhausted and indicates the persons to whom offerings are made. Since each of these two chapters fully possesses both the "person" and the "method," they are termed "double summaries.
This section is divided into two parts: first, the double summary of the persons and methods of the lower vow.

At that time, the Buddha commanded the assembly of monks from the ten directions to first offer a prayer of blessing for the donor on behalf of their parents for seven generations, wishing that they may practice the mind of meditative concentration, and only then receive the food.

[The phrase] "wishing that the seven generations of parents... was sometimes broken off, or it was expanded to include: "may they be reborn in heaven, be liberated from suffering, attain the Way, or be reborn in the Pure Land," relying solely upon this.

One offers prayers and performs incantations according to the vows of the host; however, if the donor has no specific vow of their own, the Buddhadharma naturally possesses its own methods for offering prayers and incantations.

It should be understood that these belong to those who practice recitation aloud, whereas the practice of meditative concentration—such as the method of contemplating food through the five reflections—is not related to those who recite aloud.
△ Second, the conclusion of the preceding section on the persons and methods of making offerings.

When first receiving food, one should first place it before the Buddha in a stupa or monastery; once the monks have finished reciting the *dhāraṇī* for blessings, one may then receive the food oneself.

Although the worthy and holy ones of the ten directions all possess sovereign power and can deliver those in the perilous state of being "upside-down and suspended," they are supreme and wondrous fields of merit.
As for "with liberation," this refers to those at the stage of partial realization; since their liberation is not yet ultimate, their extraction [of suffering] may be feared to lack depth.
Now, by causing them to make offerings to the Buddha, they attain the ultimate state of the Dharma King, where suffering is exhausted without exception and joy is fulfilled without limit;
thus, they are truly able to cause all who face difficulties to be free from sorrow and suffering. This double concluding passage refers to the above.
Seeking the Buddha-way to transform sentient beings below through the compassion of shared essence—the Four Great Vows—were spoken while receiving offerings from the monastic assembly at one time;
